questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman attended with flu-like symptoms. She had unprotected sexual intercourse with a casual partner 3 weeks before her symptoms began. Investigations: Fourth-generation HIV test positive Confirmatory anti-HIV-1 and anti-HIV-2 antibodies negative HIV viral load 3 million copies/mL
questions.lead_in: In addition to HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies, what does a fourth-generation HIV test detect?
questions.explanation: p24 antigen The fourth-generation HIV test is an ELISA testing for both HIV-1/HIV-2 antibodies as well as the p24 antigen (a capsid protein of the virus). Because the p24 antigen is detectable before HIV antibodies, fourth-generation tests can detect HIV infection earlier than tests that only detect HIV antibodies (third-generation tests).

questions.question: 20M that has lymphadenopathy. You do an aspiration and discover Mycobacterium tuberculosis. They do not have respiratory TB.

parts.text: What coinfection must you test for?
What are all the antimycobacterial medications you need to start and what are their durations? (4 points)
A few weeks later he has hepatitis, transaminases 6x ULN. He has not been taking any other medications. What is the most likely medication to cause his hepatitis and what do you do?
At week 12 he notes that the initial lymph node is more enlarged than it had been previously. It is nontender on examination but larger than it had been at diagnosis. What is the cause of this?

questions.model_answer:
a) Precautions: standard precautions only (no airborne isolation needed - isolated peripheral lymphadenitis without pulmonary disease is not infectious).
b) Coinfection to test for: HIV.
c) Antimycobacterial medications and durations (4 points): isoniazid x 6 months, rifampin x 6 months, pyrazinamide x 2 months, ethambutol x 2 months (2 months RIPE then 4 months INH/RIF).
d) Most likely cause of hepatitis (transaminases 6x ULN, no other meds): isoniazid (also implicating pyrazinamide and rifampin as hepatotoxic anti-TB drugs, but INH is most classically hepatotoxic). Management: stop INH (and other hepatotoxic agents PZA/RIF), monitor LFTs until they normalize/near-baseline, then sequentially reintroduce starting with rifampin, then INH, generally omitting or cautiously reintroducing PZA.
e) At week 12, enlarging but nontender node: paradoxical reaction (immune reconstitution response to effective TB treatment) - continue the same regimen without change; consider aspiration for symptom relief and corticosteroids if severe.

needs: Chapter 131 — Management of Opportunistic Infections in HIV
questions.question: HIV patient with CD4 62, viral load 250K. Immune HBV serology. Infection with PJP.

parts.text: When to start ARVs? And why?
Give 6 screening tests indicated as part of her initial HIV assessment?

cohort_answer.text:
When to start ARVs: ASAP, within 2 weeks of dx of PCP – associated with lower death. In an RCT of 282 patients with OIs other than TB, 63% of whom had definite or presumptive PCP, a significantly lower incidence of AIDS progression or death (a secondary study endpoint) was seen in subjects randomized to early (median 12 days after initiation of therapy for OI) versus deferred initiation of ART (median 45 days). Of note, no patients with PCP and respiratory failure requiring intubation were enrolled in the study, and initiating ART in such patients is problematic due to the lack of parenteral preparations and unpredictble absorption of oral medications, as well as potential drug interactions with agents commonly used in the ICU
Six screening tests: Hep C serology; Baseline labs: CBC, LFTs, renal function; Cryptococcal antigen serum; TST / IGRA; Syphilis Screening; Gonorrhea and Chlamydia screen; HPV; VZV if no clear history of chicken pox +/- immunization; Toxo; G6PD screen (in case can't use TMP-SMX); Hep A (more in MSM)

questions.question: POC HIV test with sens and spec of 99 percent.

parts.text: Calculate the the NPV and PPV in a population with point prevalence of 1%.
Provide an argument in favor and one against using this test.

cohort_answer.text: As prevalence of disease is low NPV is better. For any given test (i.e. sensitivity and specificity remain the same) as prevalence decreases, the PPV decreases because there will be more false positives for every true positive.
